opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is one of the things I think is most important about tensor logic. It goes back to an old idea in logic programming. In Prolog or Datalog, a program has a declarative reading and a procedural reading. The declarative reading says these rules are statements that are true, and the meaning of the program is everything that follows from them. The procedural reading says this is how you compute it: forward chaining, backward chaining, and so on. The beautiful thing about logic programming, when it works, is that the two coincide. You write down what's true and you get a computation for free.

In tensor logic the basic construct is the tensor equation. The left-hand side is a tensor, and the right-hand side is a join of tensors followed by a projection. That's essentially an einsum. Declaratively, that equation is just a statement. If the tensors are Boolean, it's literally a Datalog rule. The join is the conjunction in the body of the rule, and the summation over the indices that don't appear on the left is the existential quantification. If the tensors are real-valued, the same equation is a layer of a neural network, or a step of a graphical model, or a kernel machine, depending on what you put in it.

Procedurally, you can evaluate those equations in different ways, and they correspond to the familiar inference strategies. Forward chaining is just evaluating the equations in order, propagating values from inputs to outputs. That is exactly a forward pass in a neural network. Backward chaining starts from a query and works back to the tensors you need, computing only the parts that matter. That's more like what Prolog does, and it can be much more efficient when you only care about a few entries of a huge tensor.

So the point is that you don't have to choose between "I'm writing a declarative specification" and "I'm writing a procedure." It's the same program. The declarative semantics tells you what it means and lets you reason about correctness. The procedural semantics tells you how it runs on a GPU. One thing I really like is that learning fits in seamlessly. Gradients are themselves just more tensor equations, so differentiating the program gives you another tensor logic program.

There's one more layer that I find exciting. When you do reasoning in embedding space, you have a temperature parameter. At zero temperature the system does purely deductive reasoning, so the declarative semantics is classical logic, with no hallucinations. That's sound reasoning. As you raise the temperature, you get analogical and similarity-based reasoning, which is what makes deep learning powerful. You keep a single clean declarative reading of the program, and you can dial how strictly the procedure follows it. That's a big part of why I think tensor logic can be the language that finally unifies the symbolic and the connectionist traditions instead of just bolting them together.

r001.rationale: It says the tensor equation is declaratively a statement, and for Boolean tensors it is literally a Datalog rule.

r002.rationale: It describes procedural evaluation as chaining and propagating values, but does not explain the equation as a function call.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is really the heart of the whole thing, so I'm glad you asked it first. The way I think about it is that for the last seventy years, AI has essentially had two cultures that didn't talk to each other. You had the symbolic people, who cared about declarative semantics: a program is a set of statements about the world, and what it means is the set of things that logically follow from those statements. And then you had the connectionist people, and later the whole deep learning world, who cared about procedural semantics: a program is a sequence of operations, you run it, and what it means is whatever comes out the other end. And each side thought the other one had basically missed the point.

What TensorLogic does is show that these are not actually two different things. They're two views of the same object. The key observation, which in hindsight is almost embarrassingly simple, is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same operation. If you write a Datalog rule, say grandparent of X and Z if parent of X and Y and parent of Y and Z, you're joining two relations on the shared variable Y and then projecting Y away. If you write that in tensor notation, you have two matrices, you multiply them, and you sum over the inner index. That's einsum. The join is the product, the projection is the sum. Same thing, written in two notations. And once you see that, the whole wall between the two cultures just comes down.

So from the declarative side, a TensorLogic program is a set of tensor equations, and you read them the way you'd read a logic program. Each equation says: this tensor is defined in terms of these others. The meaning is the fixed point, the set of all consequences, exactly as in Datalog. You don't have to think about what runs first. And from the procedural side, exactly the same program is a computation graph. You pick an evaluation order, forward chaining or backward chaining or whatever you like, and the operations you execute are matrix multiplications and nonlinearities, which is to say they're what a neural network does. So the forward pass of a neural network is literally forward chaining in logic, with real numbers instead of booleans. Backward chaining is what you do at query time. And backpropagation is just the derivative of the forward chaining.

Now, the interesting part, and this is where I think it stops being just a cute isomorphism, is what happens in the gap between the two semantics. In pure logic you have a hard threshold: either the fact follows or it doesn't. In a neural network you have a continuous activation. And TensorLogic exposes that as a knob. You can take a tensor equation and apply a step function to the output and you've got crisp logic, where you can prove things and you never hallucinate, because every conclusion is a sound consequence of the premises. Or you can relax it, use a sigmoid or just leave it linear, and now you're doing analogical reasoning in an embedding space, where similar things have similar consequences, and you get the generalization that makes deep learning so powerful. The same program, the same declarative meaning, but the procedural realization differs in how much it's willing to extrapolate. And you can go in between, and you can learn where to sit on that spectrum.

So to answer the question directly: in TensorLogic, declarative semantics tells you what the program means and procedural semantics tells you how to compute it, and the reason that's not a trivial statement is that until now those two things lived in different fields with different math and different people. Here they're the same equation. You get to write down what you want in a form a logician would recognize, and you get to run it and differentiate it in a form that a deep learning engineer would recognize, and there is no translation step, because there's nothing to translate.

r001.rationale: It says TensorLogic equations are read like a logic program and their meaning is the fixed point of all consequences, communicating a declarative account of what the program says about the world.

r002.rationale: It describes the procedural interpretation as a computation graph evaluated through operations such as matrix multiplications and nonlinearities, but does not communicate that an equation can be interpreted as a function call.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that declarative semantics tells you what a statement means, and procedural semantics tells you how to compute with it. In TensorLogic, the bridge between those is that a logical rule can also be read as a tensor equation.

Take a simple example: if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z, then X is a grandparent of Z. Declaratively, that describes a relationship. Computationally, if you represent the parent relation as a matrix, finding grandparents looks like matrix multiplication: you combine the two parent relationships and sum over the intermediate person, Y. With Boolean operations, that gives you the logical interpretation; with numerical operations, you get a numerical computation, whose meaning depends on how you interpret those values.

The important thing is to keep the meaning separate from the execution strategy. Writing a rule shouldn’t force you to choose a particular order of operations or a particular implementation. The system can choose an efficient way to evaluate it while preserving its meaning. That’s the attraction: you can describe things at the level of logic and execute them using the machinery of tensor computation.

r001.rationale: It says a logical rule can be read as a tensor equation and that, declaratively, the rule describes a relationship.

r002.rationale: It explains procedural semantics as computation and execution, but does not describe a TensorLogic equation as a function call.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the declarative semantics tells you what a program means, and the procedural semantics tells you how to compute it. In TensorLogic, the common language is tensor equations. You can look at those equations as specifying relationships, without committing to a particular order of execution, or you can turn them into a computation that evaluates those relationships.

That’s very much the distinction we already have in logic programming: a rule has a logical meaning, but you also need an inference procedure to do something with it. And on the neural side, you have mathematical expressions that get compiled into a computational graph.

The important thing is to keep those levels separate while making the connection precise. The meaning shouldn’t depend on a particular execution strategy. Then you have room to choose an efficient implementation, exploit sparsity, reorder computations, and so on. The unification is that logical inference and neural computation can both be expressed in that same tensor language.

r001.rationale: It says declarative semantics gives a program’s meaning and that tensor equations specify relationships, conveying their declarative interpretation as statements about what holds.

r002.rationale: It describes procedural semantics as computation, inference, or a computational graph, but does not explain that an equation can be interpreted as a function call.
